The '''Benaloh Cryptosystem''' is an extension of the [[Goldwasser-Micali cryptosystem]] (GM) created in 1985 by Josh (Cohen) Benaloh.  The main improvement of the Benaloh Cryptosystem over GM is that longer blocks of data can be encrypted at once, whereas in GM each bit is encrypted individually.<ref name="COHEN-FISCHER">{{cite conference |first1=Josh |last1=Cohen |first2=Michael |last2=Ficsher |title=A Robust and Verifiable Cryptographically Secure Election Scheme |pages=372–382 |year=1985 |conference=Proceedings of 26th IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science |url=https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/elect.pdf |format=PDF}}</ref><ref name="BENALOH-THESIS">{{cite conference |first=Josh |last=Benaloh |title=Verifiable Secret-Ballot Elections (Ph.D. thesis). |year=1987 |url=https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/1987/01/thesis.pdf |format=PDF}}</ref><ref name="BENALOH-DPE">{{cite conference |first=Josh |last=Benaloh |title=Dense Probabilistic Encryption. |conference=Workshop on Selected Areas of Cryptography |pages=120–128 |year=1994 |url=https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/1999/02/dpe.pdf |format=PDF}}</ref>

==Scheme Definition==

Like many [[Public-key cryptography|public-key cryptosystems]], this scheme works in the group <math>(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*</math> where ''n'' is a product of two large [[Prime number|primes]].  This scheme is [[Homomorphic encryption|homomorphic]] and hence [[Malleability (cryptography)|malleable]].

===Key Generation===
Given block size ''r'', a public/private key pair is generated as follows:

#Choose large primes ''p'' and ''q'' such that <math>r \vert (p-1), \operatorname{gcd}(r, (p-1)/r)=1,</math> and <math>\operatorname{gcd}(r, (q-1))=1</math>
#Set <math>n=pq, \phi=(p-1)(q-1)</math>
#Choose <math>y \in \mathbb{Z}^*_n</math> such that <math>y^{\phi/r} \not \equiv 1 \mod n</math>.
:: '''Note:''' If ''r'' is composite, it was pointed out by Fousse et al. in 2011<ref name="ACRYPT">{{cite arXiv |eprint=1008.2991<!--|conference=AFRICACRYPT-->   |year=2011 |title=Benaloh's Dense Probabilistic Encryption Revisited |first1=Laurent |last1= Fousse |first2=Pascal |last2= Lafourcade |first3=Mohamed |last3= Alnuaimi|class=cs.CR   }}</ref> that the above conditions (i.e., those stated in the original paper) are insufficient to guarantee correct decryption, i.e., to guarantee that <math>D(E(m)) = m</math> in all cases (as should be the case). To address this, the authors propose the following check: let <math>r=p_1p_2\dots p_k</math> be the prime factorization of ''r''. Choose <math>y \in \mathbb{Z}^*_n</math> such that for each factor <math>p_i</math>, it is the case that  <math>y^{\phi/p_i}\ne 1\mod n</math>.
# Set <math>x=y^{\phi/r}\mod n</math>

The public key is then <math>y,n</math>, and the private key is <math>\phi,x</math>.

===Message Encryption===
To encrypt message <math>m\in\mathbb{Z}_r</math>:

# Choose a random <math>u \in \mathbb{Z}^*_n</math>
# Set <math>E_r(m) = y^m u^r \mod n</math>

===Message Decryption===
To decrypt a ciphertext <math>c\in\mathbb{Z}^*_n</math>:

# Compute <math>a=c^{\phi/r}\mod n</math>
# Output <math>m=\log_x(a)</math>, i.e., find ''m'' such that <math>x^m\equiv a \mod n</math>

To understand decryption, first notice that for any <math>m\in\mathbb{Z}_r</math> and <math>u\in\mathbb{Z}^*_n</math> we have:

:<math>a = (c)^{\phi/r} \equiv (y^m u^r)^{\phi/r} \equiv (y^{m})^{\phi/r}(u^r)^{\phi/r} \equiv (y^{\phi/r})^m(u)^{\phi} \equiv (x)^m (u)^0 \equiv x^m \mod n</math>

To recover ''m'' from ''a'', we take the [[discrete log]] of ''a'' base ''x''.  If ''r'' is small, we can recover m by an exhaustive search, i.e. checking if <math>x^i\equiv a \mod n</math> for all <math>0\dots (r-1)</math>. For larger values of ''r'', the [[Baby-step giant-step]] algorithm can be used to recover ''m'' in <math>O(\sqrt{r})</math> time and space.

===Security===

The security of this scheme rests on the [[Higher residuosity problem]], specifically, given ''z'',''r'' and ''n'' where the factorization of ''n'' is unknown, it is computationally infeasible to determine whether ''z'' is an ''r''th residue mod ''n'', i.e. if there exists an ''x'' such that <math>z \equiv x^r \mod n</math>.
